intro: Michael Laucke plays his arrangement for solo guitar of the first of the Trois Gymnopédies, marked “Lent et douloureux”. The bass, the plucked chords and the melody are all played on the one instrument.

sections.label: A · Bass and plucked chords, Lent
sections.mNote: The slow three-beat accompaniment plays before the melody enters.

sections.label: B · Melody in a lower register
sections.mNote: A held melody note sounds across changing chords.

sections.label: A′ · Opening material again
sections.mNote: Bass and chords introduce the opening melody again.

sections.label: B′ · Closing phrase in the minor
sections.mNote: The closing phrase uses a flattened third.

cues.title: Guitar arrangement, bars 1–12
cues.text: In Laucke’s arrangement one guitar plays the low bass, the accompanying chords and the melody. Satie separates the three layers, with the bass on beat one, a chord on beat two and long melody notes above. Each plucked note begins to decay before the next is played.
cues.evidence: Satie, Gymnopédie No. 1, Dover edition, bars 1–12, transcribed for Mutopia. Laucke’s arrangement and performance are credited on the recording page. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=37 ; https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Satie_Gymnopedie_No_1_performed_by_Michael_Laucke.flac
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Low held melody note, bars 17–21
cues.text: The melody drops lower and holds a single note while the chords beneath it change. The accompaniment keeps its slow three-beat step.
cues.evidence: Dover edition, Mutopia transcription, bars 17–21. The section boundary follows this passage in Laucke’s transposed arrangement; the piano score supplies the melodic and harmonic design. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=37
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening accompaniment
cues.text: The first ending closes in the major. The opening pattern of bass note and chord returns, and the melody re-enters after it as in bars 1–5. The tune is then played through a second time.
cues.evidence: Dover edition, Mutopia transcription, first ending and return to bars 1–5. The recording’s established section boundary places the return here. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=37
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second ending in minor
cues.text: In the closing melody one long note is altered, and the major third falls a semitone. Satie’s second ending, bars 40–47, closes in minor. The bass reaches the same note as in bars 32–39, with a different chord above it.
cues.evidence: Dover edition, Mutopia transcription, second ending, bars 40–47; compare bars 32–39. Laucke transposes the work from the piano original. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=37
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Held melody note over changing chords
transitions.from: A · Bass and plucked chords, Lent
transitions.to: B · Melody in a lower register
transitions.how: The melody drops to a lower held note, and the bass leaves its opening alternation. In bars 17–21 of the piano score, E minor becomes E minor seventh, then D minor under the held E. Laucke carried this change into his transposed guitar arrangement and kept the slow rhythm of bass on the first beat and chord on the second.
transitions.evidence: Dover edition, Mutopia transcription, piano bars 17–21; chord names refer to the original key. The section boundary locates the corresponding passage in Laucke’s transposed arrangement. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=37

transitions.title: The accompaniment starts again
transitions.from: B · Melody in a lower register
transitions.how: The first ending closes in major. The accompaniment then starts again with a low bass note followed by a seventh chord. This pattern continues for four bars before the melody enters. In these bars Satie leaves the upper line empty, and the bass returns to its familiar step.
transitions.evidence: Dover edition, Mutopia transcription, bars 38–39 followed by the return to bars 1–5. The guitar arrangement is transposed. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=37

transitions.title: The third falls a semitone
transitions.to: B′ · Closing phrase in the minor
transitions.how: The repeated melody takes Satie’s second ending. Its long major third is flattened, and the accompanying chords change with it. In the piano original, F♮ replaces F♯ over a repeated E bass, and the last chord is in D minor. The guitar plays the same change from major to minor in its transposed key.
transitions.evidence: Dover edition, Mutopia transcription, alternatives at bars 32–39 and 40–47; the note names describe the piano original. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=37

composer.epithet: Composer of the Gymnopédies, who asked pianists to prepare for 840 repetitions with “serious immobilities”.
facts: Paris Conservatoire; returned to study at the Schola Cantorum in 1905, aged thirty-nine
Honfleur, then Montmartre; a room in Arcueil from 1898 until his death
Cocteau, Picasso and Massine for Parade; Picabia and René Clair for Relâche
Piano miniatures, songs, ballets, Socrate and the comic Memoirs of an Amnesiac
composer.background:
In April 1912 Erik Satie told the readers of the Revue musicale S.I.M. that he preferred measuring sounds to hearing them. He reported the results of his equipment. A B♭ examined through a phonoscope was so repulsive that he called his servant to look at it; an ordinary F♯, emitted by a large tenor, weighed ninety-three kilograms. “I get more pleasure from measuring a sound than from hearing it,” he wrote. The essay belonged to his Memoirs of an Amnesiac.

He was born in Honfleur in 1866, the son of a French shipping broker and an English mother of Scottish descent. After she died in 1872, he and his brother returned from Paris to their paternal grandparents in Normandy. A local organist, Gustave Vinot, taught him music and introduced him to plainchant. Back in Paris, Satie entered the Conservatoire in 1879. Two periods of study there produced poor reports and no diploma.
